Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) has unveiled a redesigned version of its long-delayed Roadster electric sports car, featuring propulsion technology developed with SpaceX that enables the vehicle to briefly fly, rotate in midair and accelerate from zero to 60 mph in less than one second.
The demonstration took place on October 15, 2026, at a SpaceX test facility in McGregor, Texas. Tesla CEO Elon Musk said production would begin in 2028, more than a decade after the second-generation Roadster was first announced in 2017.
Tesla unveiled its next-generation Roadster on October 15, 2026, demonstrating an upside-down driving maneuver, midair rotation and jumps powered by SpaceX-developed thrusters.
The electric sports car offers claimed acceleration from 0 to 60 mph in under one second, a top speed exceeding 230 mph and a driving range of more than 300 miles.
Production is scheduled for 2028, eight years later than originally promised, with reservation deposits ranging from $50,000 to $250,000 and no confirmed final pricing.
During the event, a white two-seat Roadster drove up a curved ramp and remained attached while inverted using a fan-based suction system. The vehicle then launched into the air, rotated and landed on its wheels with assistance from integrated compressed-gas thrusters.
A second demonstration showed the car jumping over several vehicles, including a semi-truck, before completing another aerial maneuver.
This is the clmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX engineers working closely together to make something that you haven’t seen in any movie.
Tesla CEO Elon Musk
The technology combines Tesla’s electric vehicle engineering with SpaceX propulsion expertise. According to Musk, the Roadster uses ultra-high-pressure air tanks to generate thrust, allowing certain versions to overcome the traction limitations of conventional tires.
Tesla vehicle engineering chief Lars Moravy said the redesigned Roadster could accelerate from zero to 60 mph (97 kph) in under one second and reach speeds exceeding 230 mph (370 kph).
The company also claims a driving range of more than 300 miles (480 km) per charge, considerably below the approximately 620 miles promised when the second-generation model was introduced in 2017.
Tesla presented three configurations following the event. The Performance version is a two-seat electric sports car with advanced aerodynamics and a suction system. The Thrust variant adds compressed-gas acceleration thrusters, while the invite-only Rocket model features a single-seat configuration and a more extensive propulsion system designed for aerial maneuvers.
